title: When Everything Becomes a Child
gist: Samuel J. Abrams reports college students increasingly calling pets and even sourdough starters their 'children,' and links this language shift to falling US fertility and affordability anxiety among young adults. He cites Pew, CDC and IFS nine-country data showing pet-parent preference is associated with wanting nearly one fewer child.

insights.claim: Professors report that college students increasingly refer to pets, and even objects like sourdough starters, as their 'children' or 'daughters,' a language shift several colleagues have also noticed in recent months.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Signals a cultural reallocation of caregiving affection toward pets, supportive of long-run pet-economy demand.
insights.quote: her “daughter” was a sourdough starter that wasn’t rising!
insights.locator: In this one particularly memorable conversation

insights.claim: A 2023 Pew Research Center survey found 97% of American pet owners consider their pets part of the family and 51% say pets are as much family as a human member, with little variation by age.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Near-universal family status for pets underpins premium spending on pet food, health and services.
insights.quote: 97% of American pet owners consider their pets part of the family, and 51% say they are as much a part of the family as a human member

insights.claim: The author argues that equating pets with children is a category error: a pet can be beloved, but loving a pet does not make one its parent and cannot replace the meaning a child brings.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Frames the normative pushback that pro-natalist advocates will use against 'pet parent' culture.
insights.quote: Loving a pet doesn’t make me its father.
insights.locator: I’ve had pets throughout my life

insights.claim: Provisional CDC figures put the US fertility rate at 53.1 births per 1,000 women ages 15 to 44 in 2025.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Continued low US fertility feeds slower labor-force growth and shifts demand away from child-related categories.
insights.quote: Provisional CDC figures put the fertility rate at 53.1 births per 1,000 women ages 15 to 44 in 2025.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Americans are having fewer children.

insights.claim: Per Pew, the share of childless US adults under 50 who say they are unlikely ever to have children rose from 37% in 2018 to 47% in 2023, citing careers, concerns about the world and affordability among reasons.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A rising stated-intention gap suggests the fertility decline is not just delay and may persist.
insights.quote: has climbed from 37% in 2018 to 47% in 2023
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Americans are having fewer children.

insights.claim: The author hypothesizes that young people may be investing affection in animals or things because having children seems financially out of reach, though he concedes more research is needed.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: If affordability is the binding constraint, housing and childcare costs are levers for fertility and for pet-vs-child spending trade-offs.
insights.quote: I wonder if young people are investing affection in animals—or things—because having children seems so out of reach.
insights.locator: Perhaps this explains some of what

insights.claim: Students express persistent anxiety about jobs, rent and whether they will ever own a home, making it hard to explain how child-rearing could work for them.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Housing affordability and job insecurity remain central to young-adult household formation delays.
insights.quote: they constantly share with me their concerns about jobs, rent, and whether they will ever be able to own a home
insights.locator: Even with tenure and time to prepare

insights.claim: Even a tenured professor in New York found the costs of raising children daunting and delayed having children for financial and professional reasons.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: High-cost metros amplify fertility delay among educated professionals.

insights.claim: A 2021 study by anthropologist Shelly Volsche of Boise State University found childless adults reported stronger pet attachments and were more likely to call themselves their pets' parents.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Childless households are the core high-attachment, high-spend segment for pet products.
insights.locator: As it happens, there is some interesting research

insights.claim: A 2017 study by sociologist Andrea Laurent-Simpson of Texas Woman's University suggested relationships with pets could reinforce decisions to delay or forgo children.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Implies a feedback loop where pet ownership and low fertility reinforce each other.
insights.locator: As it happens, there is some interesting research

insights.claim: IFS survey data from nine countries show young adults who agree 'I would rather be a pet parent' want nearly one fewer child than those who don't, a gap that persists after controlling for income, education, relationship status and age.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A cross-country, control-robust association links pet-parent identity to lower desired fertility.
insights.quote: reported wanting nearly one less child than those who did not
insights.locator: More recently, the Institute for Family Studies

insights.claim: The nine-country IFS finding cannot establish direction: preferring pets may lower desired fertility, or people already wanting fewer children may be drawn to pet parenthood.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Caution against treating pet adoption as a causal fertility suppressor in forecasts.
insights.locator: More recently, the Institute for Family Studies

insights.claim: The author contends young people hear mostly about the hardships of parenting—exhaustion and expense—and too little about its joys, which shapes their intentions.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Suggests cultural narrative, not only economics, influences fertility, a target for pro-family campaigns.
insights.quote: too many have only heard about the hardships
insights.locator: I wish more of my students heard

insights.claim: A new IFS report indicates communal support from friends and family increases the likelihood of wanting and eventually having children, so society should make childbearing easier and speak proudly about why children matter.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Points to community and policy support as fertility levers, relevant to pro-natal policy watchers.
insights.quote: communal support from friends and family can actually help increase the likelihood of wanting and eventually having kids
insights.locator: We should make it easier for younger generations
